strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: learning generative models directly from corrupted observations without clean data, across natural and scientific imaging domains.

Generalizes Denoising Score Distillation (DSD) to broader corruption operators, including blur, random inpainting, super-resolution, and multi-coil MRI, and shows compatibility with several corruption-aware pretraining objectives (Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion).

Empirical results are relatively strong across many settings: RSD consistently improves over the corresponding teacher models in all reported tasks, achieves one-step generation, and is directly distilled from publicly available checkpoints in some cases.
Includes a practical contribution for unsupervised model selection via Proximal FID and demonstrates distillation data efficiency and inference speedup.
Provides a theoretical attempt to explain the regularization effect, characterizing global minimizers of a simplified score-distillation objective in a linear Gaussian setting.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core framework largely combines existing components—score distillation (SiD), Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, and Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion—with the natural modification of corrupting generated samples before training the fake diffusion model. The paper does not introduce a fundamentally new distillation mechanism.

The theoretical analysis is limited and overclaimed. It only studies a rank-1 linear Gaussian model with perfect score estimation, assumes a specific low-rank linear generator parameterization, and does not compare the distilled student to the pretrained teacher. The general claim of recovering the clean covariance eigenspace is not proven beyond rank 1; the kernel(A) component is arbitrary unless a minimum-norm solution is selected, which is not enforced by the actual training algorithm.

For non-invertible corruption operators, the distillation objective is not clearly justified: using w_g = A(x_g) to match the teacher's corrupted-data score only constrains A(G(z)) to follow the corrupted distribution p_Y. For super-resolution and high-rate inpainting, this does not by itself guarantee recovery of the clean distribution p_X, and the paper does not provide a convincing explanation of why the one-step generator learns clean samples beyond empirical observation.

Evaluation is relatively narrow: natural-image experiments are only on CelebA-HQ 64x64, with no other standard natural-image benchmarks and no multiple training seeds or error bars. The paper lacks key ablations, such as the effect of the generated-sample corruption step, the choice of corruption-aware pretraining objective within the same task, or alternative distillation losses (e.g., KL vs. Fisher).

Baseline comparisons are incomplete in places. EM-Diffusion (few-shot) outperforms RSD on noisy Gaussian deblurring (51.33 vs. 76.98 FID), and some teacher baselines are very weak (e.g., Ambient Tweedie for noisy inpainting at FID 319.34), making the reported gains less informative. Comparisons to other distillation or corruption-robust generative methods are missing.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: no code is released, training requires 100M image iterations on 8 A100 GPUs, and several implementation details are deferred to appendices. This makes independent reproduction difficult.

Presentation clarity could be improved. The algorithm for general corruption is not always easy to follow, and notation around the distillation loss, corrupted generated samples, and the role of Ambient Tweedie is somewhat confusing.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: learning generative models from corrupted data without clean samples, with potential impact in scientific imaging and inverse problems.

Integrates the proposed RSD framework with several existing corruption-aware diffusion pretraining objectives, including Standard Diffusion, Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, and Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion, showing flexibility across corruption types.

Reports strong empirical gains in several settings, especially multi-coil MRI, where RSD improves FID over teacher models and L1-EDM across acceleration rates, and also provides a one-step generator with substantial inference speedup.
Proposes Proximal FID as a practical model-selection proxy when clean data are unavailable, which is a useful direction for corrupted-data generative modeling.
Includes a theoretical attempt to study distilled generation under linear low-rank Gaussian assumptions, which is a reasonable starting point for understanding score distillation with corruptions.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited and incremental: RSD mainly applies the existing SiD score-distillation framework to teachers trained with existing corruption-aware diffusion objectives. The core distillation loss and corruption-aware pretraining ingredients are not new, and the extension from DSD to general corruptions is largely a straightforward composition of known components.

The theoretical analysis is only weakly connected to the proposed method. It assumes perfect score estimation of the corrupted distribution, considers a rank-1 linear Gaussian model, and does not model the teacher model or the distillation dynamics. It also does not prove that RSD improves over the teacher or that distillation acts as a regularizer; instead, the result shows a noise-dependent scaling of the recovered eigenvector, so the claim that RSD recovers the clean eigenspace is overstated.

The evaluation is insufficient for a top-tier conference. Natural-image experiments are limited to CelebA-HQ 64x64, with no higher-resolution or broader natural-image benchmarks. Baselines are limited, and EM-Diffusion (few-shot) outperforms RSD on noisy Gaussian deblurring, which weakens the claimed consistency of improvements.

The paper conflates unconditional generative modeling from corrupted training data with image restoration/reconstruction. RSD trains an unconditional one-step generator and does not condition on a given corrupted observation, so it does not solve the restoration inverse problem for specific inputs. Qualitative figures describing corrupted inputs and generated outputs as pairs are misleading in this context.

The method requires knowledge of the corruption operator and noise level to corrupt generated samples during distillation and to choose the pretraining objective. The limitations section claims robustness to unknown corruption operators, but the algorithm and experiments depend on applying the same corruption process to generated data, so this claim is not well supported.

The data-efficiency argument is not fully convincing: distillation still requires 50-100 million image iterations after pretraining, and comparisons to teacher training need more careful accounting of total compute. Reproducibility is also limited by missing code, incomplete distillation hyperparameters, and reliance on public checkpoints.

strengths: The paper proposes Restoration Score Distillation (RSD), a clear two-phase framework that extends score distillation to general corruption operators such as blurring, inpainting, super-resolution, and Fourier-domain MRI corruption, without requiring clean data at any stage.

Empirically, RSD consistently improves over its corruption-pretrained teacher models across diverse noiseless and noisy restoration tasks on CelebA-HQ and multi-coil FastMRI, often by large FID margins. It also surpasses the few-shot EM-Diffusion baseline in most settings, despite using no clean images.

The framework is modular and compatible with existing corruption-aware diffusion methods (Standard Diffusion, Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion), including distillation directly from public checkpoints. This makes the approach practical and easy to integrate.

The one-step generator yields substantial inference acceleration (about 25x) and the distillation stage is relatively data-efficient, surpassing teacher performance within roughly 12M image iterations in several tasks. The proposed Proximal FID is a useful practical proxy for model selection when clean validation data is unavailable.

The theoretical analysis in the linear Gaussian regime provides an interesting characterization of global minimizers, showing that RSD recovers the clean data eigenspace up to noise-dependent scaling, which helps interpret score distillation as an implicit regularizer.
The manuscript is well organized, with detailed algorithms, proofs, implementation details, and qualitative results in the appendix.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: RSD combines existing corruption-aware pretraining objectives with SiD-style distillation, and the main algorithmic change is to corrupt generated samples using the same operator during distillation. The core components are largely inherited from prior work.

The theoretical analysis is quite restrictive: it assumes a rank-one linear Gaussian model, linear corruption, perfect score estimation, and a low-rank linear generator. It does not analyze optimization dynamics, finite-sample effects, or nonlinear corruptions, and it does not directly prove that distillation yields a smaller Wasserstein distance than the pretrained teacher.

There is a mismatch between the theory and the noisy experimental setup. The theorem uses the score of y = A(x) + sigma * epsilon with additional diffusion noise, whereas the noisy experiments use Ambient Tweedie, whose objective targets the distribution of A(x) with diffusion noise only. Thus the theory does not fully cover the main noisy regime studied empirically.

Experimental evaluation is limited in scale and diversity: natural-image experiments are only on CelebA-HQ 64x64, with no results on CIFAR, ImageNet, FFHQ, or higher resolutions. Scientific evaluation is limited to one MRI dataset. This narrows the demonstrated generality of the claims.

Important ablations are missing. There is no systematic ablation isolating the effect of corrupting generated samples in the distillation stage, the choice of pretraining objective, the number of fake-diffusion steps, or SiD hyperparameters. It is therefore unclear how much of the improvement comes from RSD specifically versus standard distillation or the teacher checkpoint.

Only FID is reported for most generative evaluations; precision/recall or other diversity metrics are absent. Since distillation can improve FID partly by reducing sample diversity, additional metrics would strengthen the claim that RSD produces genuinely higher-quality and diverse samples.

The MRI pipeline still requires coil sensitivity maps obtained via ESPIRiT calibration, which may rely on additional autocalibration data. This slightly weakens the claim of learning entirely from corrupted observations in that setting.

The distillation stage itself is computationally expensive (50-100M image iterations on 8 A100 GPUs), so the practical data efficiency claim is relative to the expensive teacher pretraining rather than being efficient in absolute terms.

strengths: Strong empirical study: RSD consistently improves FID over corruption-aware diffusion teachers and several zero-/few-shot baselines across denoising, deblurring, inpainting, super-resolution, and multi-coil MRI, often with large margins.

Practical and modular framework: it cleanly combines existing corruption-aware diffusion pretraining objectives with score distillation, making it easy to swap in different corruption operators or pretraining losses.

Demonstrates clear benefits beyond sampling acceleration: one-step generators can outperform their multi-step corrupted-data teachers, and the paper provides extensive ablations on data scale, noise misspecification, distillation losses, and downstream inverse problems.

Includes useful practical contributions such as Proximal FID for model selection without clean data, with experiments showing it often tracks true FID, plus detailed implementation and efficiency reporting.
Theoretical analysis in the appendix attempts to justify the surprising quality improvement, including linear Gaussian bounds and general Fisher-divergence guarantees under assumptions.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited: the method largely applies existing score distillation (SiD) to generators trained after existing corruption-aware diffusion pretraining, with the corruption pipeline reused during distillation. The core technical idea is natural but incremental.

The theoretical support is useful but narrow: the main quantitative results rely on idealized linear/low-rank Gaussian models, perfect score estimation, and restrictive capacity/optimization assumptions, so they do not fully explain practical nonlinear, non-invertible, high-dimensional corruption settings.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: while RSD improves over teachers consistently, it does not dominate all few-shot methods in every setting (e.g., noisy Gaussian deblurring), and the paper sometimes overstates generality across corruption regimes.

Proximal FID is promising but not fully reliable: in several general-corruption settings the selected checkpoint has a non-trivial FID gap to the oracle-selected checkpoint (e.g., noisy random inpainting and super-resolution), so model selection under corruption remains only partially solved.

Reproducibility is incomplete for review: the abstract mentions code availability but no working link is provided, and some key experimental choices (e.g., exact validation/model-selection criterion used for main tables) are not fully specified.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat uneven: several baselines are taken from prior papers or reproduced under different assumptions, and ablation of distillation losses uses default hyperparameters from other methods, limiting conclusions about which loss is intrinsically best.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: learning generative models solely from corrupted observations, with potential applications in medical and scientific imaging where clean data are scarce.

It provides a broad empirical study across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, AFHQ-v2, MRI), corruption types (denoising, Gaussian deblurring, random inpainting, super-resolution, Fourier undersampling), and noise levels, with generally large FID improvements over corruption-aware diffusion teachers.

The proposed Proximal FID is a simple and practical model-selection metric for corrupted-data regimes, and the one-step generator yields substantial inference speedups over multi-step diffusion teachers.
The appendix attempts a theoretical analysis in stylized linear Gaussian settings, which is a useful starting point for understanding why distillation can improve sample quality beyond acceleration.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: RSD is largely a pipeline that combines existing corruption-aware diffusion pretraining objectives with an existing score-distillation method (SiD). The main new ingredient is to apply the same corruption operator to generated samples during distillation, which is intuitive but incremental rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The central claim of learning the clean distribution from non-invertible corruptions is not adequately justified. For operators with nontrivial kernels (blur, downsampling, inpainting), matching measurement-space distributions—as the distillation loss and Algorithm 1 do—does not identify p_X. The theory itself allows kernel(A) perturbations and only provides a Wasserstein bound under an explicit minimum-norm/regularization assumption that is not enforced in the proposed algorithm.

The theoretical results are highly restrictive: they assume linear Gaussian low-rank data, perfect score estimation, and idealised distillation losses. They do not directly establish the claimed behaviour of the proposed finite-data SiD-based algorithm, and thus provide limited support for the central empirical claims.

Evaluation and comparison issues: the corruption-aware teachers are not always optimized for clean generation; in some noisy restoration settings RSD is worse than few-shot EM-Diffusion (e.g., noisy Gaussian deblurring), which weakens the claim that RSD consistently surpasses prior methods. More ablations are needed to disentangle gains from distillation, corruption-aware pretraining, and hyperparameter tuning.

Clarity and reproducibility weaknesses: the manuscript contains inconsistent citations/years, a missing code URL, minor notation errors, and relies heavily on appendix material. Reproducibility would be strengthened by releasing code/checkpoints and specifying all hyperparameters clearly.

strengths: Introduces Restoration Score Distillation (RSD), a unified and modular framework for learning one-step generative models directly from corrupted observations, covering denoising, deblurring, inpainting, super-resolution, and multi-coil MRI without clean training data.

Reports consistent and often substantial FID improvements over corruption-aware diffusion teachers across multiple datasets, noise levels, and corruption types, with some zero-shot results surpassing few-shot baselines that use clean images.

Demonstrates practical benefits: one-step sampling yields up to 30x speedup, distillation surpasses teacher quality in significantly fewer iterations, and the method integrates with existing corruption-aware diffusion objectives.
Provides several useful ablations and practical components, including Proximal FID for model selection under corruption, unknown-noise handling, data-size scaling, and distillation-loss comparisons.

Includes theoretical analysis in stylized linear Gaussian and low-rank settings, with extensions to general corruptions and conditions under which distillation can reduce Wasserstein or Fisher divergence relative to the teacher.
The problem setting is important for scientific and medical imaging, and the empirical evaluation spans natural images, restoration tasks, and FastMRI, which strengthens the practical relevance.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is mostly the combination of existing corruption-aware diffusion pretraining with existing score distillation (primarily SiD); no fundamentally new distillation objective or corruption-aware training mechanism is introduced.

For non-invertible corruption operators, the method's ability to recover the clean distribution is not fully justified in practice. If the teacher is trained only on corrupted measurements, distillation can only identify the clean distribution up to the nullspace of the corruption; the paper relies on implicit or minimum-norm regularization, but this is not clearly enforced or validated.

Algorithmic details are unclear in important places. For example, Algorithm 1 updates the generator using $x_\theta = y_\theta = \mathcal{A}(G_\theta(z))$ in the distillation loss; it is not explained how gradients through a non-invertible or dimension-reducing operator enable recovery of missing clean-space components, especially when the teacher models only corrupted data.

Experimental scale is limited to relatively low-resolution images (32x32 and 64x64) and MRI; there is no evaluation on higher-resolution or large-scale text-to-image settings where score distillation is most commonly tested.

Some comparisons are not fully conclusive. Under noisy Gaussian deblurring, RSD underperforms the few-shot EM-Diffusion baseline (76.98 vs. 51.33 FID), so the claim of consistent superiority over few-shot methods should be qualified.

The theoretical results rely on strong assumptions such as perfect score estimation, linear low-rank Gaussian data, and bounded noise schedules. The gap between these idealized analyses and practical neural-network training is large.

Potential reproducibility and fairness concerns remain: baseline hyperparameters may not be extensively tuned, teacher sampling schedules for some corruptions may not be optimal, and key implementation details for initialization and gradient flow under general operators are deferred or underspecified.
